clue.text: Around middle of afternoon sleeper becomes active

indicators.note: Around tells us the sleeper's letters go round the other piece

parts.note: a sleeper is a dormant secret agent, a spy

indicators.note: middle of picks out the central letter of the nine-letter word afternoon

explanation.surface: A drowsy person perks up halfway through the afternoon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sleeper' looks like a dozing person but is the spy kind; SPY goes round R, the middle letter of 'afternoon'.
explanation.definitionFit: Spry describes someone lively and nimble, a synonym of active.

clue.text: One buying mostly undiluted whisky after beer?

indicators.note: mostly means the word for undiluted loses its final letter

parts.note: undiluted means pure
a chaser is a short of spirits drunk after a beer

explanation.surface: A drinker orders a near-neat whisky to follow a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the last letter of the word for undiluted; the question mark flags that 'whisky after beer' defines its piece by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A purchaser is a buyer, someone who pays for goods.

clue.text: Play Chuck Berry record

definitions.meaning: a comedy by George Bernard Shaw of this title
a 1964 rock and roll single by Chuck Berry of the same title

explanation.definitionFit: The title belongs both to a Shaw stage comedy and to a Chuck Berry hit single.

clue.text: Cricketer said to appear with hat on

indicators.note: said tells us we want a word that sounds like the synonym of to appear

parts.note: to appear means to seem
a bowler is a hard round felt hat

explanation.surface: A man is spoken of as turning up wearing a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: SEEM sounds like SEAM. A seam bowler is a cricket bowler who makes the ball deviate off its stitched seam; a bowler hat is the British domed felt hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A seam bowler is a type of fast-medium bowler in cricket, so a cricketer.

clue.text: Workers employed in dockyard usually turned up

indicators.note: turned up says the hidden letters are read backwards, as from bottom to top in a down clue
employed in says the letters are found within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Labourers are generally taken on at the docks.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Workers employed' as definition, leaving the hidden word with no indicator; 'employed in' is the containment signal and 'Workers' alone defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sudra are the labouring caste in the traditional Hindu system, the workers.

clue.text: Learner misses top grade, so lost for words

indicators.note: misses says one letter is dropped from the word for the top grade

parts.note: alpha is the top grade in marking, as in alpha plus
L is the learner driver's plate letter
sic is Latin for so or thus

explanation.surface: A student fails to get an A and is left speechless.
explanation.walkthrough: ALPHA without L gives APHA, then SIC. 'Learner misses top grade' reads as a student falling short, but the learner is the letter missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphasia is loss of the ability to use language, so an aphasic person cannot find speech.

clue.text: Kind of squash goat's head?

parts.note: a goat butts, so it is a butter, and the possessive links it to its head
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A whimsical question about what a goat's head might be called.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits the playful reading: a goat is something that butts, and a goat's head is the butter's nut.
explanation.definitionFit: Butternut is a variety of winter squash with pale orange flesh.

clue.text: Song from G Gershwin's Paris collection

indicators.note: collection says these letters are gathered and rearranged

parts.note: the name with its S taken as written

explanation.surface: A tune taken from a George Gershwin songbook about Paris.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collection' sounds like a set of songs but signals the anagram of G GERSHWINS PARIS. Whispering Grass is a 1940 song made famous by the Ink Spots.
explanation.definitionFit: Whispering Grass is a well-known popular ballad, so a song.

clue.text: Have meal at home: nauseating sandwiches

indicators.note: sandwiches says the word nauseating holds the letters inside it

explanation.surface: Dining in is suggested because sandwiches are sickening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sandwiches' looks like food, fitting the meal, but is the containment signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To eat in is to dine at home rather than going out.

clue.text: Crazy to make a song and dance

parts.note: a round is a song in which voices enter in turn with the same tune
the Twist is a 1960s dance craze

explanation.surface: Making a fuss is madness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make a song and dance' is an idiom for a fuss, but here it is literally a song and then a dance. Round the twist is British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Round the twist is British slang for mad or deranged.

clue.text: Guerrilla leader hates wild animals

parts.note: Che Guevara led guerrillas in the Cuban revolution

indicators.note: wild says the letters of hates run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: A rebel commander loathes untamed beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild animals' looks like one phrase, but 'wild' rearranges HATES into ETAHS.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheetahs are big cats, the fastest land animals.

clue.text: Grow with experience principally

parts.note: exp. is the abbreviation of experience, its principal letters
with means and, joining things together

explanation.surface: Developing as one gains know-how.
explanation.definitionFit: To expand is to increase in size, a synonym of grow.

clue.text: A former disc jockey's turned out

indicators.note: turned says the disc jockey's name with its S is read backwards

parts.note: John Peel was a long-serving BBC Radio 1 DJ who died in 2004, and his name with the possessive gives the letters

explanation.surface: A one-time radio presenter has been ejected from his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'turned' reverses PEELS to SLEEP and 'out' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone out cold or out for the count is unconscious, as is a sleeper.

clue.text: Fish one served about noon, maybe

parts.note: perch is a freshwater fish

indicators.note: about says the serve's letters go round the abbreviation for noon

parts.note: an ace is a serve in tennis that the receiver cannot touch

explanation.surface: A fish dish is perhaps being served around midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'served' suggests a restaurant, but the thing served is a tennis ace.
explanation.definitionFit: Perchance is an old-fashioned word for perhaps.

clue.text: Study Greek female dramatist

parts.note: to con is to study or learn by heart
Eve, the first woman, stands for any female

explanation.surface: A student examines a Greek woman playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek female dramatist' reads as one person, but the dramatist is the Restoration playwright William Congreve.
explanation.definitionFit: William Congreve wrote Restoration comedies such as The Way of the World.

clue.text: Lout never trained as soldier in WWI?

indicators.note: trained says the letters are drilled into a new order

explanation.surface: A thug who never had any drill joined up in the Great War.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trained' suits a soldier but signals the anagram. Britain's army in the early First World War was raised from enlisted civilians, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Before conscription in 1916 the British army relied on men who signed up of their own accord.

clue.text: Got successfully treated by expert

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert
a patient successfully treated is cured

explanation.surface: Someone was healed by a specialist.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a medical success, but 'Got' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To procure something is to obtain it, so got.

clue.text: Day one has with girl in part of Ireland

parts.note: gal is a casual word for girl

explanation.surface: A man spends a day with a girlfriend in an Irish county.
explanation.definitionFit: Donegal is a county in the far northwest of the Republic of Ireland.

clue.text: Confused mass of seaweed

definitions.meaning: a large brown kelp of northern shores

explanation.definitionFit: A tangle is a twisted knot of things, and also the name of a kelp, Laminaria.

clue.text: Left a foreign companion to catch a boat

indicators.note: to catch says the other letters take the following article inside them

parts.note: un is French for a
CH stands for Companion of Honour

explanation.surface: A friend from abroad departs in a hurry to make a ferry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to catch a boat' reads as travel; in fact L, UN, CH hold the second A.
explanation.definitionFit: A launch is a large motorboat.

clue.text: Love a way-out broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast says we hear the words spoken rather than written

parts.note: a way out is a door

explanation.surface: Adoring an eccentric radio show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'way-out' looks like slang for odd, but is a door: 'a door' said aloud is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore someone is to love them deeply.

clue.text: Figures behave amorously shortly after retiring

indicators.note: retiring means going back, so the run is read backwards

parts.note: snog is British slang for kiss and cuddle
anon means soon

explanation.surface: Shapes cuddle briefly before going to bed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retiring' suggests bedtime after romance, but reverses SNOGANON.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonagons are nine-sided polygons, geometric figures.

clue.text: Famous announcement of Heath's disappearance?

parts.note: no in the sense of none present, gone
Ted is the first name of Edward Heath, UK Prime Minister 1970 to 1974

explanation.surface: A well-known statement on a politician vanishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No Ted' is what one might announce after Ted Heath vanished; the question mark marks the playful split.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means well known or celebrated, a synonym of famous.

clue.text: Item of luggage: unexpectedly 14 has it

indicators.note: unexpectedly says the letters turn up in a surprising new order

parts.note: 14 across, the dramatist

explanation.surface: A bag the playwright surprisingly owns.
explanation.walkthrough: Anagram of CONGREVE (the answer at 14) plus HAS IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A small bag holding what one needs for a single night away is a kind of luggage.

clue.text: Able to afford Harley Street treatment, say, got better after depression

definitions.text: Able to afford Harley Street treatment

indicators.note: after says the second piece follows the word for depression

parts.note: a well is a hollow in the ground, a depression

indicators.note: say signals a word that sounds like the one for recovering

parts.note: got better means healed

explanation.surface: Someone rich enough for private doctors recovered after feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: Harley Street is the London street of expensive private doctors; 'depression' suggests low mood but is a WELL.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-heeled means wealthy, and private consultants cost a lot.

clue.text: Confident about backing America in recession

indicators.note: backing says the word for about comes behind, supporting what precedes it
in recession means going backwards, so America's letters are reversed

parts.note: US is short for the United States
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: An economist feels sure about supporting the USA through a downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in recession' turns the abbreviation for America round, and 'backing' sets the word for about behind it. 'recession' looks economic but signals the reversal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sure means feeling certain, a synonym of confident.
